scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: Original B2 assessment items analysing the same reading passage from a fresh angle. NOT copied from the practice question bank.

tabs.title: Meaning and Implications
tabs.description: Interpret the message and its assumptions.

tabs.title: Reasoning and Structure
tabs.description: Evaluate how the writer supports and qualifies claims.

tabs.title: Applying the Ideas
tabs.description: Apply the author's reasoning to new realistic situations.

questions.q: Why might constructive advice be less useful to a student who usually receives high grades?
choices: They may treat a comment about a piece of work as a judgement about their intelligence.
They are unlikely to understand detailed teacher comments.
Their teacher will not suggest improvements to successful students.
They already know exactly how to improve without guidance.
questions.explanation: Paragraph one distinguishes advice about work from a judgement about the learner's identity.

questions.q: What is the student's likely purpose in rewriting one paragraph before meeting the teacher?
choices: To replace the original grade with a new one.
To demonstrate that the teacher's criticism was necessarily unfair.
To try a more effective way of connecting evidence and the main claim.
To avoid discussing weaknesses in the original argument.
questions.explanation: The revision is a trial of how the reasoning could be made clearer, not a request to change the existing mark.

questions.q: What potential problem is suggested by a marking system that favours a narrow writing style?
choices: A logically argued essay might be undervalued because of its style.
All students will earn equally high marks.
Teachers will stop assessing whether evidence is relevant.
Writing style will become completely irrelevant to evaluation.
questions.explanation: Paragraph three notes that assessment criteria themselves may favour a limited range of expression.

questions.q: Why does the writer contrast two reactions to the same disappointing essay result?
choices: To prove that the grade was calculated incorrectly.
To separate the unchanged result from the different opportunities for future learning.
To demonstrate that grades should be removed from essays.
To suggest the student should choose the more emotionally satisfying reaction.
questions.explanation: Both reactions leave the existing mark unchanged, but only one helps the learner improve.

questions.q: What important qualification does the writer introduce in the third paragraph?
choices: Only highly experienced students can benefit from criticism.
Students should question any grade that disappoints them.
Feedback itself may be mistaken, so questions and evidence still matter.
The best feedback focuses on writing style rather than the argument.
questions.explanation: The author recognises the fallibility of teachers and grading systems and advocates precise clarification.

questions.q: Why are coaches, colleagues and friends mentioned near the end?
choices: To rank personal advice above teachers' feedback.
To argue that feedback is useful only outside formal education.
To show that the principle applies beyond school, even when advice is incomplete.
To explain why personal relationships prevent criticism.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph transfers the argument to other settings while preserving the need to examine evidence.

questions.q: A student believes the teacher missed a link between two claims in an essay. What is the most constructive response?
choices: Ignore the comment because teachers sometimes misunderstand.
Point to the relevant passages and ask where the connection remains unclear.
Copy the teacher's wording into the essay without further discussion.
Ask for a higher grade without revisiting the argument.
questions.explanation: A specific, evidence-based question allows both the student and teacher to examine the issue.

questions.q: A classmate argues, 'Criticism that makes you upset cannot help you learn.' Which response best fits the article?
choices: Discomfort and the usefulness of advice are separate questions.
A learner should always enjoy useful criticism.
Unpleasant comments are accurate more often than pleasant ones.
Criticism should be followed without checking its accuracy.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph separates emotional discomfort from deciding what is worth testing.

questions.q: A student revises an essay only to persuade the teacher to raise the old mark. Which learning benefit is being overlooked?
choices: Memorising the teacher's favourite vocabulary.
Improving the approach to organising arguments in future assignments.
Writing fewer sentences in every future essay.
Getting teachers to avoid criticism in the future.
questions.explanation: The example focuses on improving future performance even when the original grade is unchanged.

questions.q: A coach identifies a weakness but has not seen the athlete's full situation. What should the athlete do according to the writer's reasoning?
choices: Ignore the coach's observation completely.
Apply the advice immediately because expertise guarantees accuracy.
Examine the observation against further evidence before deciding what to change.
Ask a friend to replace the coach's judgement without further investigation.
questions.explanation: The author says partial observations can still be valuable, but their usefulness must be tested against evidence.
